summary: Frogs overwhelm Egyptian homes, but after Moses prays for relief Pharaoh hardens his heart again. Aaron then strikes dust that becomes lice, a sign the magicians cannot copy; swarms of flies follow with Goshen set apart, and Pharaoh’s limited permission for sacrifice ends in another refusal after the insects are removed.
whyItMatters: The pattern of demand, affliction, plea, relief, and renewed refusal becomes clear. The magicians’ limits and Goshen’s protection sharpen the distinction Pharaoh is repeatedly asked to recognize.

context.author: Exodus names no writer of the finished book, though it depicts Moses writing particular words. Later tradition ascribes the Torah to him; its composition remains debated.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through its story of rescue, covenant, and worship; this chapter names no narrower first audience.
context.date: The book gives a relative story sequence but no secure external year for the events. The dating and formation of its finished text remain debated.
context.setting: Egyptian homes, fields, and Pharaoh’s court, with Goshen named as protected from the swarms of flies.
context.literaryForm: Three linked plague episodes with repeated warnings, human and animal effects, negotiation, intercession, and reversal.

before.text: The Nile was made undrinkable for seven days while Pharaoh returned home and Egyptians dug for water. The next demand brings affliction from the river into homes.

here.text: Frogs, lice, and flies disrupt Egypt; Pharaoh asks for prayer and offers limited permission, then rescinds it after relief.

after.text: The following chapter moves to Egyptian livestock, bodily boils, and a warned hailstorm, while Goshen or Israel is again distinguished.

outline.heading: Frogs enter homes and work spaces
outline.note: The demand is refused and frogs spread; Egyptian magicians reproduce the sign.

outline.heading: Prayer, stench, and reversal
outline.note: Pharaoh promises release, Moses prays, and Pharaoh hardens his heart after respite.

outline.heading: Lice from dust
outline.note: Aaron’s blow affects people and animals; magicians fail and call it God’s finger.

outline.heading: Flies, with Goshen set apart
outline.note: Moses warns Pharaoh, and swarms corrupt Egypt while Israel’s region is distinguished.

outline.heading: A restricted offer withdrawn
outline.note: Pharaoh negotiates distance, requests prayer, and refuses again once flies depart.

keyVerses.text: But when Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart, and didn’t listen to them, as Yahweh had spoken.
keyVerses.why: The verse explicitly assigns the renewed hardening to Pharaoh after he experiences relief.

keyVerses.text: Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is God’s finger;” but Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he didn’t listen to them, as Yahweh had spoken.
keyVerses.why: The court magicians acknowledge a limit they cannot overcome while Pharaoh remains unmoved.

keyVerses.text: I will set apart in that day the land of Goshen, in which my people dwell, that no swarms of flies shall be there, to the end you may know that I am Yahweh on the earth.
keyVerses.why: Goshen’s distinction is given as a sign that Yahweh is active within the land.

questions.question: How do frogs change ordinary life?
questions.answer: They spread from the river into bedrooms, beds, ovens, and kneading troughs, then die in heaps that make the land stink. The sign affects household life and food preparation, not only Pharaoh’s palace.

questions.question: Why does Pharaoh change course after the frogs die?
questions.answer: He had promised release if Moses prayed for relief, but the narrator says he saw a respite and hardened his own heart. The chapter reports this reversal without giving a fuller private explanation of his thought.

questions.question: What does “God’s finger” mean in the magicians’ response?
questions.answer: After failing to produce lice, the magicians use this phrase to attribute the sign to divine power. It is their speech to Pharaoh, and even their acknowledgment does not make him listen.

questions.question: What is new about the flies and Goshen?
questions.answer: The warning explicitly separates the land where Israel lives from the places flies will corrupt. Yahweh says this division will show he is present in the land, and the swarms then arrive in Egyptian houses.

questions.question: Is Pharaoh’s offer to sacrifice in Egypt the requested release?
questions.answer: No. Moses and Aaron have requested a wilderness journey, while Pharaoh first offers sacrifice within Egypt and then allows only a journey that does not go far. His proposals preserve control over the terms and are withdrawn after relief.

questions.question: Why does Moses say sacrifice in Egypt is unsafe?
questions.answer: He says what Israel would sacrifice is an abomination to Egyptians and fears they would stone the worshipers. The chapter records his stated reason without describing the precise sacrificial animals or a later Egyptian attack.

questions.question: What part does prayer play in the plague episodes?
questions.answer: Pharaoh asks Moses to entreat Yahweh over frogs and later flies; Moses prays, and the afflictions cease. Those answered requests do not secure lasting permission because Pharaoh refuses again.

glossary.def: The relief Pharaoh sees after frogs die, immediately before he hardens his heart again.
The creatures produced when Aaron strikes the dust, affecting people and animals.
The area where Israel lives and which is set apart from the fly swarms.
